newsitem.title: USA: Clinton unveils clothing-industry sweatshop pact.
newsitem.headline: Clinton unveils clothing-industry sweatshop pact.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday endorsed an apparel industry code of conduct barring the use of child labour and other sweatshop conditions at shoe and clothing factories used by U.S. firms around the world.

Clinton said at a White House ceremony the new code of conduct will help improve the lives of millions of garment workers around the world. "As has now been painfully well-documented, some of the clothes and shoes we buy here in America are manufactured under working conditions which are deplorable and unacceptable," he said.

The code of conduct sets a maximum mandatory work week of 48 hours plus 12 hours of mandatory overtime, with at least one day off in every seven-day period. It requires clothing companies and their subcontractors to pay at least the minimum wage or prevailing industry wage, whichever is higher, and bars companies from employing children under the age of 15, or 14 in countries that permit it.

The agreement calls for monitors to conduct independent reviews of participating company policies and practices. It also calls for establishment of an industry association that will implement the agreement and try to recruit more companies to join in following the code of conduct.

The agreement was the product of a presidential task force made up of U.S. clothing makers such as Nike Inc, L.L. Bean, and Liz Claiborne Inc., labour unions and human rights groups, which banded together to recommend steps to ensure products were not made under exploitative conditions.

"This partnership has reached an agreement that will significantly reduce the use of sweatshop labour over the long run," Clinton said. "It will give American consumers greater confidence in the products they buy."
Companies adhering to the code will be able to label their products with a seal of approval.
The National Consumers League, a group formed 100 years ago to fight sweatshops, participated in the White House event and issued a statement calling the agreement a "monumental achievement."

Robert Silk, director of the Robert F. Kennedy Centre for Human Rights, called the agreement "an important down payment on eliminating child labour and sweatshop conditions from the apparel industry."
But critics said the agreement does not go far enough and basically calls for practices already adopted by companies.

"We don't see that this gets us any closer to eliminating any sweatshops," said Medea Benjamin of San Francisco-based Global Exchange, which has criticised practices at factories used by Nike. "Companies already have codes, already have independent monitors, yet we still have sweatshops."

The initiative came about after talk show host Kathie Lee Gifford, who lends her name to a line of clothing, was severely criticised last year for labour practices at factories making products sold under her name.

Paul Charron, chairman and chief executive of Liz Claiborne, who co-chaired the task force that developed the code, said at the White House that its success will depend on recruiting other firms to make it an industry-wide standard.
Clinton said the agreement was "just the beginning because even though there are some very impressive and big companies represented on this stage, there are some which are not."
